analogy.p: Picture two kinds of train carriage, A and B, each with a coupler at both ends that must be bolted together. Every time a coupler on an A joins a coupler on a B, a tiny bolt-cover is thrown away; that thrown-away bit is the water lost. The carriages alternate A, B, A, B to make one long train, the polyester, and each join is an ester link. It breaks down because real functional groups are atoms that react and rearrange (the H and OH come from different monomers), rather than parts that are simply bolted together.

bullets: **Condensation polymerisation:** monomers with two functional groups join, usually losing a small molecule such as water.
The small molecule lost each time is called the **by-product** (for polyesters it is water, H2O).
Each monomer must have **two** functional groups so that the chain can grow from **both ends**.
The simplest polymers: two different monomers, each with **two identical functional groups** (e.g. a diol and a dicarboxylic acid).
Addition polymers need a **C=C**; condensation polymers do **not** need C=C at all.
This point is marked **triple (Chemistry only)** content, so check your course covers it.
core.p: In **condensation polymerisation** monomers with two functional groups react together, and every time two monomers join a small molecule is lost, usually **water**. The word 'condensation' refers to this loss of a small molecule when molecules combine. The product is a long polymer chain, and the small molecules lost are a second product. This is the main difference from addition polymerisation, where nothing is lost and the polymer is the only product. The simplest condensation polymers are made from **two different monomers**, each with **two of the same functional group**.

bullets: **Alcohol group** = –OH; a molecule with two of them is a **diol** (e.g. ethane-1,2-diol).
**Carboxylic acid group** = –COOH; a molecule with two of them is a **dicarboxylic acid** (e.g. hexanedioic acid).
Block diagram: diol = **HO–[A]–OH**; dicarboxylic acid = **HOOC–[B]–COOH**.
Mr of ethane-1,2-diol C2H6O2 = 24 + 6 + 32 = **62**.
Mr of hexanedioic acid C6H10O4 = 72 + 10 + 64 = **146**.
Link: alcohols and carboxylic acids are in the organic chemistry topic; a carboxylic acid plus an alcohol makes an **ester** (with water) in the presence of a catalyst.
core.h: Functional groups involved: alcohol and carboxylic acid
core.p: A **diol** is a molecule with two **alcohol** groups (–OH), one at each end of a carbon chain, for example ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH. A **dicarboxylic acid** has two **carboxyl** groups (–COOH), one at each end, for example hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH2)4COOH. The functional groups are what react, while the carbon chain between them does not change. A useful way to draw them is as HO–[A]–OH and HOOC–[B]–COOH, where the boxes A and B stand for the rest of each molecule. Writing the monomers in this block form keeps you focused on the ends, which is exactly where the reaction happens.

bullets: **Step 1:** the diol HO–A–OH and the diacid HOOC–B–COOH come together.
**Step 2:** the –OH of the diol reacts with the –COOH of the diacid, and **H2O is lost**.
**Step 3:** an **ester link** –O–C(=O)– joins the two monomers: HO–A–O–C(=O)–B–COOH.
**Step 4:** the free –OH at one end and the free –COOH at the other end react with more monomers, losing more water each time.
**Step 5:** a very long chain forms with alternating A and B units joined by ester links.
**Products:** polyester **and** water (one water per ester link formed).
core.h: How a polyester forms, step by step
core.p: A diol reacts with a dicarboxylic acid. The –OH group on the end of the diol combines with the –COOH group on the end of the acid: the H from the –OH and the OH from the –COOH leave together as a molecule of **water**, and the oxygen of the alcohol bonds to the carbon of the carbonyl group. The new group formed, –O–C(=O)–, is an **ester link** (ester linkage). The molecule formed still has an –OH at one end and a –COOH at the other, so it can react again with another monomer at each end. Repeating this thousands of times gives a long chain called a **polyester**.

bullets: **Ester link** = –O–C(=O)–, also written –COO–.
Repeat unit in block form: **–[O–A–O–C(=O)–B–C(=O)]–** (one diol part and one acid part).
The repeat unit has **lost atoms** compared with the two monomers: the H and OH lost as water.
The polymer backbone contains **ester links** as well as carbon atoms (unlike addition polymers, which only have carbon in the backbone).
Draw bonds that **go through the brackets** at each end, and include **n**.
The A and B can be any carbon chain, so **polyesters can have different properties** depending on the monomers.
core.h: The ester link and the repeat unit
core.p: The ester link is –O–C(=O)–: one oxygen joins the chain, and the carbon also has a double bond to a second oxygen (the carbonyl group). The repeat unit of a polyester made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid contains **one piece from each monomer**, joined by two ester links at the ends: –[O–A–O–C(=O)–B–C(=O)]–. It is drawn in brackets with bonds through the brackets and the letter n, just as for an addition polymer. The repeat unit does not have exactly the same atoms as the two monomers added together, because the atoms in water (H and OH) have been lost from the ends.

bullets: Look for **–O–C(=O)–** in the chain = **ester link** = **polyester**.
Monomers: one with **–OH at both ends** (diol) and one with **–COOH at both ends** (dicarboxylic acid).
Do not expect to **recall** specific polyester monomer names; use the information in the question.
If a question gives a **different pair of monomers**, apply exactly the same idea: lose a small molecule where the functional groups react.
The by-product is **water** for a diol + dicarboxylic acid.
Some polyesters are used to make **fibres for clothing and plastic bottles**; you do not need to know these for the mark scheme.
core.p: A condensation polymer made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid is called a **polyester** because it contains ester links. You are expected to recognise this from the diagram of the polymer (look for –O–C(=O)– in the backbone) and from the monomers (an –OH at each end of one molecule and a –COOH at each end of the other). Students are **not required** to recall the names or structures of specific polyester monomers beyond the ones given in a question; you will be shown the structures or functional groups. Be able to use the block diagram to explain the reaction in any question.

bullets: **Step 1:** write HO–A–OH and HOOC–B–COOH.
**Step 2:** remove an **H** from the alcohol –OH and an **OH** from the –COOH (these make H2O).
**Step 3:** join the O (from the alcohol) to the C of the carbonyl: **–O–C(=O)–**.
**Step 4:** repeat at both ends and put the repeat unit in **brackets with n**.
Check: every ester link must show **C=O** and the **O** joining the chain.
Check: the repeat unit includes **both** an A part and a B part.
core.h: Drawing the polymer from the monomers
core.p: To draw the polymer, write the two monomers in block form and join them with an ester link, removing the –H from the –OH of the diol and the –OH from the –COOH of the acid. Show enough of the chain (at least two repeat units or the repeat unit in brackets) and include the continuation bonds. In a diagram question, you may be asked to draw the ester link only, or the repeat unit, so read the instruction carefully. Always show the **C=O** in the ester link; leaving it out turns it into an ether, which is a common error.

bullets: **Step 1:** mark each **ester link** –O–C(=O)– in the chain.
**Step 2:** break the bond between **O and C(=O)** at every ester link.
**Step 3:** put **H** on the O end to make **–OH**; put **OH** on the carbonyl end to make **–COOH**.
**Step 4:** you get a **diol** (–OH at both ends) and a **dicarboxylic acid** (–COOH at both ends).
Check: the number of atoms in the two monomers should equal the repeat unit **plus two H2O**.
Always draw/say **two** functional groups on each monomer.
core.h: Working out the monomers from a polyester
core.p: To find the monomers, locate each ester link in the polymer and break it. Between the oxygen and the carbonyl carbon, the bond breaks: add an **H** to the oxygen to make an –OH (alcohol), and add an **OH** to the carbonyl carbon to make a –COOH (carboxylic acid). This is the reverse of the polymerisation reaction (in reality this reverse reaction is called hydrolysis). Then draw the two monomers: a molecule with an –OH at each end, and a molecule with a –COOH at each end. Check that each monomer has two functional groups.

bullets: One **ester link** formed = one **H2O** lost.
Chain of **4 monomers** has **3 links**, so **3 H2O** lost.
Chain of 2n monomers has **(2n − 1)** ester links and loses **(2n − 1) H2O**.
Mass of polymer = **total mass of monomers − mass of water lost**.
Example: Mr of the dimer HO–A–O–C(=O)–B–COOH from ethane-1,2-diol and hexanedioic acid = 62 + 146 − 18 = **190**.
Atom economy of the polymer < 100%, because **water** is a by-product.
core.h: Water lost and the mass of the polymer
core.p: Every time an ester link forms, one molecule of water is lost, so the total mass of the polymer is less than the total mass of all the monomers used. For a chain made from n diol molecules and n diacid molecules, there are 2n monomers joined end to end, which makes 2n − 1 ester links, so 2n − 1 molecules of water are lost. For very long chains this is almost 2n, so the repeat unit (one diol part and one acid part) has lost two H2O compared with the two monomers. This also means the **atom economy** is below 100% if you only count the polymer as the useful product.

bullets: Addition: monomers have **C=C**; condensation: monomers have **two functional groups**.
Addition: **no by-product**; condensation: **small molecule (water)** lost.
Addition: **usually one type of monomer**; condensation (polyester): **two different monomers**.
Addition: **repeat unit has the same atoms as monomer**; condensation: **atoms lost**.
Addition backbone: **C–C only**; polyester backbone contains **ester links**.
Both need the word **'polymer'** and the idea of **many monomers**; both are drawn with a **repeat unit** in brackets.
core.p: Both types make long chains from many small monomers, but the monomers, the bonds formed and the products are different. Addition polymerisation needs monomers with a **C=C** and gives only the polymer. Condensation polymerisation needs monomers with **two functional groups** (such as –OH and –COOH) and gives the polymer plus a small molecule. You must be able to compare the two, so learn these differences. Also remember that polyesters have **ester links** in the backbone, whereas addition polymers have a backbone of **carbon atoms only**.

bullets: **Amino acid:** has an **–NH2** group and a **–COOH** group in one molecule.
Amino acids join by **condensation polymerisation** to form **polypeptides** (proteins), losing **water**.
Polyester: **two monomers**, same type of group on each; polypeptide: **one type of molecule** with two different groups.
Starch and cellulose are natural polymers (from glucose).
Link to biology: **digestion** breaks these polymers down using enzymes (the reverse process, **hydrolysis**).
Link to using resources: polyesters can be **recycled**, but many are not biodegradable.
core.h: Links: amino acids, proteins and natural polymers
core.p: The same idea of condensation polymerisation explains how natural polymers form. **Amino acids** have two different functional groups, an amino group (–NH2) and a carboxyl group (–COOH), and they join in condensation reactions to make **polypeptides** and then proteins, again losing water. This is covered in the next spec point (amino acids and DNA). Other natural polymers include starch and cellulose. The key idea to carry forward is: join two functional groups, lose a small molecule, build a chain. Notice that for amino acids a **single monomer** has two different functional groups, whereas for the polyester you need **two different monomers**.

bullets: **Type of reaction:** say 'condensation polymerisation' (not 'condensation' alone).
**Describe 2–3 marks:** monomers with two functional groups; they join; water (small molecule) lost; polymer formed.
**Draw a polyester (2–3 marks):** ester link –O–C(=O)–, repeat unit, bonds through brackets, n.
**Name the group:** –OH alcohol, –COOH carboxylic acid, –O–C(=O)– ester link.
**Compare (3–4 marks):** C=C vs two functional groups; one vs two monomers; no by-product vs water.
**Calculation:** sum Mr of monomers, subtract 18 for each water lost.
core.h: Exam technique and common question types
core.p: Questions on this topic are usually short: identify the type of polymerisation, name the functional groups, show the ester link, or say what is lost. For longer 'describe/explain' questions, give the **monomers (two functional groups each)**, **what is lost (water)**, and **the polymer formed (polyester with ester links)**. Always use the phrase **'small molecule'** or name it as water. When asked to contrast with addition polymerisation, make a comparison for each point (not two separate paragraphs) so that the mark scheme points are clear. For calculation marks, show the Mr of each substance and subtract the water.

exam: **Identify (1 mark):** 'condensation polymerisation' because a small molecule/water is lost.
**Name the by-product (1 mark):** water, H2O (for a diol and dicarboxylic acid).
**Name the functional groups (1–2 marks):** –OH (alcohol/hydroxyl) and –COOH (carboxylic acid/carboxyl); the link is an ester.
**Describe how a polyester forms (3–4 marks):** the diol and dicarboxylic acid each have two functional groups (1); –OH and –COOH react (1); water lost (1); ester link formed/polymer chain (1).
**Draw the repeat unit (2–3 marks):** ester link with C=O (1); A and B units (1); brackets, bonds through them, n (1).
**Work out the monomers (2 marks):** break at the ester link; HO–A–OH and HOOC–B–COOH.
**Compare addition and condensation (3–4 marks):** C=C vs two functional groups; one product vs two; one monomer vs two; repeat unit.
**Calculation (2–3 marks):** Mr sum minus 18 per water; show working.
**Command words:** 'State' = short answer; 'Describe' = steps; 'Explain' = steps with 'because'.
**6-mark questions:** define, functional groups, reaction step, ester link, water lost, polyester features, comparison with addition.

mistakes.r: Condensation monomers have two functional groups (e.g. –OH, –COOH); a C=C is for addition polymers.
mistakes.w: Saying the monomers have a C=C double bond.

mistakes.r: A small molecule (water) is lost each time two monomers join.
mistakes.w: Saying nothing is lost or the polymer is the only product.
Leaving out the C=O in the ester link or drawing –O–.

mistakes.r: Each monomer needs two functional groups so the chain can grow at both ends.
mistakes.w: Giving the monomers with only one functional group.

mistakes.r: The term is 'condensation polymerisation'; it has nothing to do with gas to liquid.
The repeat unit has lost atoms (the H and OH that make water).
mistakes.w: Saying the repeat unit is the same as the two monomers added together.

mistakes.r: Draw brackets with continuation bonds and n.
mistakes.w: Forgetting n or the bonds through the brackets in the repeat unit.

mistakes.r: O end gets H (–OH); the C=O end gets OH (–COOH).
mistakes.w: Adding H and OH the wrong way when working back to monomers.

summary: AQA (triple science) wants you to know that **condensation polymerisation** uses monomers with **two functional groups** each; when they join they usually lose a small molecule such as **water**, forming a polymer. The simplest case is a **diol** plus a **dicarboxylic acid** making a **polyester** with ester links. You must recognise the type of reaction, show how the monomers join, say what is lost, and work back from the polymer to the monomers. It matters because polyesters and (in the next point) proteins are made this way.

terms.d: Polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups join together, usually losing a small molecule such as water.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
A very large molecule made of many repeating units joined by covalent bonds.
The group of atoms that gives an organic molecule its characteristic reactions.
The hydroxyl functional group found in alcohols.
The functional group of carboxylic acids.
A molecule with two alcohol (–OH) groups, one at each end.
A molecule with two carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups, one at each end.
The –O–C(=O)– (–COO–) group formed when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid.
A condensation polymer made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, containing ester links.
The smallest repeating group of atoms in a polymer chain, drawn in brackets with n.
A substance formed alongside the main product, here water.
Polymerisation of monomers with C=C bonds with no other product.
A molecule with an amino group (–NH2) and a carboxyl group (–COOH) that can form polypeptides.
A polymer made from amino acids joined by condensation polymerisation.

worked.q: Ethane-1,2-diol (HOCH2CH2OH) reacts with hexanedioic acid (HOOC(CH2)4COOH) to form a polyester. Name the other product and calculate the Mr of the molecule formed when ONE of each monomer joins. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16) [3 marks]
steps: Joining one of each loses one H2O (Mr 18): 62 + 146 − 18 = 190.

worked.q: A polyester chain is made from 10 diol molecules and 10 diacid molecules (the same monomers as above). How many water molecules are lost and what is the Mr of the chain? [3 marks]
steps: 20 monomers joined end to end make 19 ester links.

worked.ans: The diol has two –OH groups and the dicarboxylic acid has two –COOH groups (1). An –OH group reacts with a –COOH group (1) and a molecule of water is lost (1). This forms an ester link, –O–C(=O)–, joining the monomers, and the reaction repeats at both ends to form a long polyester chain (1).
